title: Quantum Computing and the Future of Finance: Exploring How Quantum Technology Impacts Financial Analysis and Forecasting
journal_or_venue: Isrg J Econ Bus Manag (ISRG Publishers)
abstract_summary: This mixed-methods study examines how quantum computing affects financial analysis and forecasting using a survey of 100 financial analysts/IT specialists and in-depth interviews with 20 experts. Results indicate that 70% of respondents expect improved forecasting accuracy, while major barriers include high infrastructure costs, skills gaps, and security/privacy concerns; the paper recommends investment in infrastructure, training, and new security protocols to enable adoption.
methodology_description: The study used a mixed-methods design combining qualitative and quantitative approaches. Qualitative data were collected via semi-structured, in-depth interviews with twenty purposively selected experts (academic scholars, industry practitioners, IT and cybersecurity specialists) chosen for their professional experience and domain expertise; interviews were coded and analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify themes and patterns (coding, theme identification, thematic interpretation). Quantitative data were obtained from an online structured questionnaire completed by a purposive sample of 100 financial analysts, researchers, and IT specialists; the survey included closed-ended items (Likert scales, multiple-choice and simple response formats). The quantitative data were analyzed descriptively using tables and charts and inferentially with t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SPSS and Microsoft Excel. Validity and reliability measures included a pilot test of the questionnaire, data triangulation across multiple expert sources, and comparing findings to secondary literature (books, journal articles, databases). The study also used secondary/library sources to contextualize primary findings. Participant selection emphasized diversity in academic background and professional experience; instruments aimed to probe forecasting accuracy, infrastructure challenges, risk reduction potential, application areas, and security/privacy concerns. No computational/quantum algorithm experiments or financial-market datasets were used.

results_summary: This mixed-methods empirical study (100 survey respondents and 20 expert interviews) finds broad optimism among finance and IT professionals that quantum computing could improve forecasting accuracy and address complex optimization tasks (majorities: 70% believe accuracy improves; 80% underline advantages for optimization/simulation). However, significant adoption barriers were reported — infrastructure costs and complexity, training gaps, and serious security/privacy concerns (55% rate infrastructure barriers high/very high; 65% are highly concerned about security). Recommendations focus on infrastructure investment, workforce education, new security protocols, and continued empirical testing. While expert opinion highlights theoretical advantages for modeling nonlinearity and real-time multidimensional forecasting, technical attributions to specific quantum algorithms (e.g., Shor) for forecasting tasks are inconsistent with established algorithmic roles and remain unproven in practice.

contradictions: The paper attributes applicability of Shor's algorithm and (ambiguously) the 'Harrow algorithm' to portfolio simulation and risk-assessment tasks; this is a factual misattribution—Shor is for integer factoring and HHL (Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd) targets linear systems with strong caveats—so the algorithm-application mapping is incorrect.

The strong expert optimism (e.g., 80% say QC can solve problems beyond classical reach) is presented alongside acknowledgements of severe infrastructure, skills, and security barriers, creating a tension between claimed near-term transformational impact and the lack of empirical/technical evidence or validated scaling paths (contradiction with practical scalability).
